title: SLOs and error budgets
summary: How to say how reliable a service should be, measure it from the user's side, and use the gap to 100% to decide when to ship and when to fix.

blocks.p: Nothing is 100% reliable. Networks drop packets, disks fail and deploys have bugs. Each extra step toward 100% costs more and slows every release.
Without an agreed target, every incident is a crisis and every release is a risk argued from scratch. Product wants features, operations wants stability, and neither has a number to point to.

list: **SLI**, service level indicator. A measurement of what users experience, usually a ratio: good requests divided by valid requests. For example, requests that succeeded in under 300 ms.
**SLO**, service level objective. The target for an SLI over a window, such as 99.9% of requests good over 30 days.
**SLA**, service level agreement. A promise to customers with a penalty, such as a refund. It is set looser than the SLO, so you hear about trouble before you owe money.

blocks.p: Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by ten times.

blocks.caption: Downtime allowed in a year at each target. 99.9% allows under 9 hours. 99.999% allows about 5 minutes.

blocks.p: An SLO of 99.9% means 0.1% of requests may fail. That 0.1% is the **error budget**. While budget is left, the team ships features and takes risks. When it runs out, the team slows releases and works on reliability until the service is back within target.
This turns an argument into a rule both sides agreed in advance.

blocks.caption: The error budget for a 30-day window, as failed requests and as equivalent full-outage time assuming even traffic.

blocks.p: A request that needs several services in a row only succeeds if all of them do. Their availabilities multiply, so the whole is less reliable than any part.

blocks.caption: Availability of a request that needs every service in a chain, if each fails on its own.

blocks.p: Alert when the budget is being spent fast, not on every error. The rate of spending is the **burn rate**. A burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget in exactly the window. A rate of 14.4 spends 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour, which is worth paging on when confirmed by a short window such as 5 minutes.

list: **The SRE book defines the terms.** Google's [Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) chapter explains SLIs, SLOs and SLAs, and why 100% is the wrong target.
**Write an error budget policy.** The SRE workbook's [example policy](https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/) says what the team does when the budget runs out, agreed before it happens.

**Burn-rate alerts.** The workbook chapter [Alerting on SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/) works through alert designs, and uses a 14.4 burn rate over one hour as a page-worthy threshold.
**Measure from the user's side.** An SLI taken at the load balancer or client sees failures that a server's own metrics miss, such as requests that never reached it.
An SLI measures what users experience. An SLO sets a target for it. An SLA adds a penalty and is looser.
The gap between the SLO and 100% is the error budget. Spend it on releases; when it runs out, fix reliability.
Services called in a chain multiply their availabilities.
Alert on how fast the budget burns, not on single errors.
